prime.problem: One merge makes a 616-byte paragraph only 20 tokens shorter. A useful tokenizer needs thousands of merges, chosen automatically, and a clear boundary between the text it learned from and the model that will use it.
prime.fits: The previous card wrote get_stats and merge and did one merge by hand. This card wraps them in a loop that trains a whole tokenizer, then steps back to show where that tokenizer sits relative to the LLM.
prime.goal: Write the training loop, predict roughly how compression grows with more merges, and explain why the tokenizer's training text decides which languages and formats come out short.

attend: Why does each merge in the list remove fewer tokens than the one before it?
Which merges reuse an earlier minted token, and what does that force about the order of merges?
What exactly is kept after training: the shortened ids, or something else?
Why can't the LLM's loss adjust the merges once the LLM starts training?
Why does the blog-trained tokenizer barely shrink the Korean line?

must: Each pass merges the currently most common pair → every later pair is rarer (646 → 144 removals) → compression grows ever more slowly with vocab_size (1.27× at 276, 2.15× at 512)

A minted id goes back into ids → later passes can pair it again ((259, 256) = 'the␣') → merges form a forest → a merge only makes sense after its parents exist, so the dict's order is part of the tokenizer

Merges are chosen by counting pairs in the tokenizer's own training text → strings that are frequent there get short → text the tokenizer rarely saw (Korean for a blog-trained tokenizer) stays about one token per byte and eats the LLM's context
BPE training is counting, not gradient descent → it's done once and frozen before the LLM trains → the LLM only ever sees ids, and a token that's rare in the LLM's data keeps an untrained embedding
elevated: Each pass rescans the whole sequence (get_stats then merge) → training cost grows with text length × number of merges → this card's 20 merges on 24,597 bytes finish in about a second, while minbpe's 256 merges on 185,768 bytes took 10.9 s on your M3
reference: the Colab names: tokens (raw bytes), ids (the merged copy), num_merges = vocab_size - 256, idx = 256 + i
the print format merging (101, 32) into a new token 256
the exact 20 merges and their counts on the blog post

compress.prompt: Without scrolling up, explain in 3–5 sentences how a BPE tokenizer is trained and why it's a separate stage from the LLM. Or draw the loop and the two-stage diagram from memory.
checklist: start from the 256 byte values; repeat: count adjacent pairs, merge the most common into a new id
run vocab_size − 256 times; what you keep is the ordered merges dict
each merge helps less, so compression grows slowly (20 merges: 1.27×)
merged tokens can merge again, so the order of merges matters
the tokenizer is trained once on its own text; that text decides what gets short; the LLM later sees only ids

retrieve.q: Explain why the output of tokenizer training is the merges dict and not the shortened ids list.
answer: ids is just the training text compressed, useful only to measure the ratio
merges is a rule you can apply to any new text (encode) and invert (decode)
its insertion order records which merges must happen first

retrieve.q: Walk through passes 1 and 20 on the blog post: what does get_stats return, which pair wins, and what happens to ids?
answer: pass 1: counts all byte pairs; (101, 32) 'e␣' wins with 646; ids goes 24,597 → 23,951; merges[(101, 32)] = 256
pass 20: counts pairs that now include minted ids; (259, 256) 'th'+'e␣' wins with 144; ids ends at 19,438; merges[(259, 256)] = 275

retrieve.q: You're building a tokenizer for an LLM that will read mostly English but must serve Korean users well. What do you put in the tokenizer's training text, and what does each choice cost?
answer: more Korean in the tokenizer text → more Korean merges → shorter Korean sequences and more of it fits in context
at a fixed vocab_size, those merges come at the expense of English ones, so English gets slightly longer
raising vocab_size instead grows the embedding table and output layer
Korean-heavy tokens that the LLM rarely sees in its own data may end up undertrained

compare.q: The training loop and the encode loop both call get_stats and merge repeatedly. What's fundamentally different about how each picks the next pair, and what would go wrong if encode used training's rule?
answer: training picks the most frequent pair in its text (max by count) and mints a new id
encode picks the pair with the lowest merge index (min over merges) and mints nothing
using counts at encode time would apply merges in a text-dependent order, so the same string could tokenize differently in different documents and could try merges whose parents don't exist yet

compare.q: Training the bigram LLM vs training the tokenizer: both are called training. What does each optimise, how does each update, and how does each fail?
answer: LLM: minimises a loss by gradient descent, many small updates to real-valued weights
tokenizer: greedy counting, one irreversible discrete merge per step, no loss and no gradient
LLM failure: underfitting or overfitting the loss
tokenizer failure: merges fitted to the wrong text mixture, so other languages or formats stay long

predict.q: You have the 20 merges. A new text contains the␣ but in it the pair (259, 256) happens to be rarer than (105, 110). When you encode it, should you apply merges in the order of their counts in the new text, or some other order? Commit before revealing.
predict.answer: Training order (lowest merge index first), regardless of counts in the new text. Token 275 is defined as 259 + 256, and those only exist after merges 1 and 4 have been applied. Counts in the new text are irrelevant: the tokenizer is frozen. That's the encode card's min over merge index.
